The Great Crested Flycatcher (Myiarchus crinitus) is a medium-sized tyrant flycatcher widely distributed across eastern North American deciduous forests. Like many cavity-nesting passerines, its life history is characterized by altricial young and a relatively fast pace of development compared to other members of the Tyrannidae family. This lag between physiological maturity and first reproductive effort is likely related to the challenges of territory acquisition and the need to accumulate sufficient energy reserves for successful nesting. This altricial condition necessitates an extended period of intense parental care and provisioning before the young achieve independence.

Growth during the nestling stage is rapid, with the young feathering out and achieving flight capability at a relatively young age. Fledging, defined as the permanent departure from the nest cavity, occurs at 15 days after hatching [tx = 15 days after hatching] under the species' typical active metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].
